"Trim the sails! Oars in the water! Careful now, men!"

Ulfric's fathers voice carried over the fishing vessel that for three days had sailed into the western sea. On the return journey they would have to row, for seven days, and Ulfric was not looking forward to his turn at the oar but he would sooner die than hint at protest. Now he stood with his father at the bow, watching the Magi's castle draw near. Behind him the grunts and invocations were whispered - the men were nervous, just as he was. Even his father kept glancing back over the men at the door to the cargo hold, as if he could be anything but sure of his hold.

"The water, Father," Ulfric spoke the question. The strange shapes and shadows in the waves, and currents that seemed to swell from the surface of the ocean, were like nothing he'd ever before seen. His father flashed a smile, assured and assuring. "It's some of the Magi's power, Ulfric. You can rest assured he know's we're coming."

As if to verify the words, the sea ahead of them lit up with a glowing foam, wending through the ragged tumbled stones that would threaten to hull their boat, and the air seemed to thicken into sheets of ice or glass, reflecting, refracting, and warping strangely the sky dark with threatened snow. A light came on at the top of the Magi's castle, and far below, but still high in the wall, appeared a great doorway of what could only be mithril. Ulfric's father turned from the bow to walk up the aisle to where his steward sat cradling the eye-pad.

"Does he tell you what of our stock he wants for trade?" Ulfric's father asked, quietly, but his voice carried for the silence of the crew.

The steward stroked the ice-like surface of the eye-pad - itself obtained from the Magi years before Ulfric was born - and nodded perfunctorily. "As usual, he will be fond for our cream and cheese. Five and twenty years is a long time to go between desserts. Other foodstuffs he will accept, the ores and wood...", the steward's voice belied the preciousness ascribed to that, "...he values as well. And of course..."

At this the steward's eyes met the chieftain's and an unspoken message was carried between them. Ulfric fell backward against the railing as the ship suddenly stopped, and then - did his senses deceive? - rose into the air. The horizon tilted around as the ship was drawn alongside the looming door which - and here Ulfric surely was deceived - melted into rivulets which then rose like winding vines to climb the stony wall.

A platform awaited their cargo, already laden with boxes wrapped in the strange glossy leaves - paper, Ulfric remembered - and standing beside them the queerest of dolls. Half as tall as a man, and balancing impossibly on a tiny ball and narrow waist, it resembled ever so vaguely the mechanical bird that had stopped flying the year before and Ulfric had seen packed in the hold while the men kept with their wives and the sisters prayed for a safe journey. Even as the relation occurred to Ulfric, the mechanical man raised its arm in a parody of greeting and spoke.

"Greetings, Ranfric son of Elfric son of Ulfric!" The doll's voice, warbling like the birds that lay eggs on the rocks, was nearly as surprising as hearing his name being spoken. But instantly Ulfric knew two things - that the Ulfric so named had been his great grandfather, and that the doll was not a man at all, but what the men called a robot.

"Hail, Magi, and messenger of the Magi." Ulfric's father spoke not to the machine but to the high wall towering overhead. "We come at the appointed time, bringing gifts to trade."

"And what do you have to trade?" This time the voice was different. It was clearly the voice of a man and not the machine, though that was what spoke. The man sounded amused, and indulgent, and maybe tired. Ulfric knew that this was the voice of the Magi.

"This you already know, Magi." Ulfric's father answered in the manner of a ritual. "And you know what we seek."

"Yes, Ranfric, I do. You require the centennial consignment of mithril. You also wish for an everfire, a new scouting bird, and one hundred vials of lifewater, do you not?" The Magi's voice raised slightly in volume, as if he heard the murmurs of excitement from the men in the boat accompanying this last. The dark season had brought with it a slow sickness, and many of the old and young were sent to the dark. The lifewater was said to cure all ills, even the wounds of the flesh that could come from the bears or the sharks or the accidents that were a part of life, and had always been spoken of with only the hushed tones of reverence. The oldest sister even called it by the sacred and cursed name: "nanotek".

"You know this is true," Ulfric's father spoke when the murmurs died down. There was a silence, then, for a long time. Ulfric didn't speak, he barely breathed. He watched the men, who themselves looked to the sky or the deck and mouthed silent prayers. He looked at the steward, whose face was a study in composure. He looked to his father, who looked resigned to the fate that awaited them.

Finally the robot spoke again, and this time it was in the warbling voice of birdsong, as sparkling lines split and glowed on the floor next to the wrapped boxes in a large circular sigul. Ulfric saw, in the glowing lines, pictures of flowers, starbursts, and seashells. "I've been instructed to allow you to consign all available plastisteel sheet, one fusion battery with heating element, one scouting drone with delta-level control system, and two vials of human regenerative elixir in exchange for the cargo listed on your manifest. Please indicate compliance by unloading into the designated area."

At first the murmurs were again quiet, but soon rose in an ugly wave, as curses and sworn violence were voiced. Ulfric felt the flicker of fear in his stomach as some men even stood, and brandished their hooks and knives in gestures of potent rage at the silent figure of the machine balanced inhumanly still beneath the massive wall. Even the air itself seemed to be angry, as jagged shards of air pressed in around them, feeling to threaten to rent them into pieces. Finally, Ulfric's father cleared his throat.

"Only two, Magi? You wouldn't reconsider?" At this, the robot spoke again, with no change in inflection or rhythm, "I've been instructed to allow you to consign all available plastisteel..."

"Even had we brought you an apprentice?"

"...with heating element, one..." Thus came the recitation to a halt, and the silence now felt pregnant with hope, yet Ulfric felt the prickle of fear even stronger now.

"Father?" Ulfric spoke, with a quaver that he hated in his voice, "What do you mean? An apprentice?"

"The boy? You mean to sell your own son, Ranfric?" And the laughter of the Magi that followed echoed not just from the robot but from all the air and sea and rock around them, and Ulfric's questions and now pleading were unheard in the cacophony. Suddenly, there was silence, and Ulfric felt even more than terror a hot shame at the tears that squirted down his cheeks.

"Very well, I accept. Leave the boy with the rest."

Ulfric could no more fight against the arms and oars that kept him on the rock than he could help his fight to escape his fate. At last, when the ship was a distant speck on the horizon and his voice was hoarse and raw, a new rumble was felt in his feet, and he turned to see where before there was just a solid rock wall a doorway where stood a shadowed figure.

As it strode into the now empty platform, casting a shadow even over the glowing lines of sigul, the figure loomed higher than the castle had, even higher than the sky, and Ulfric was so afraid he could barely breath and would have leapt from the platform into the sea had the space which was moments ago open suddenly a solid door again. But then, light shined on the Magi's face, and, even if it was not like any face Ulfric had ever seen before, at least it was human.

The Magi's face was unlined and clean shaven, but drawn with glowing siguls, and his eyes were silver mirrors, and his gaze was ageless. He wore a simple robe, in the style of the sisters, but this one was the color of the scales of the rainbow fish - silver, red, green, and yellow, and all other colors besides. The magi bent down, and spoke in a quiet voice.

"Hello, apprentice."
